---
name: interface-forge-extension
description: Design, implement, redesign, audit, and harden production browser-extension UI for Manifest V3 action popups, Chrome side panels, Firefox sidebars, options and onboarding pages, content overlays, new-tab pages, DevTools panels, toolbar actions, badges, commands, and permission flows across Chromium, Firefox, and Safari. Use for extension interface design, constrained-surface adaptation, cross-browser manifests and themes, lifecycle-safe state, accessibility, CSP, permission/privacy review, responsive behavior, or store-readiness. Do not use for ordinary websites, native-mobile apps, or backend-only extension work with no UI impact.
---

# Interface Forge Extension

Build browser-extension interfaces as privileged, short-lived and cross-browser surfaces. Keep permissions minimal, executable code local, state durable and every surface useful within its real size and lifecycle.

## Operating contract

1. Inspect the existing manifest(s), build system, browser targets, permissions, service worker/background model, storage, messages, content scripts and UI surfaces before designing.
2. Select the smallest surface that supports the task. Do not force a multi-step workflow into an action popup.
3. Treat web pages, messages, captured content and remote responses as untrusted data. Render through safe DOM/text APIs and validate message shape and sender.
4. Persist meaningful state outside popup/side-panel memory. Register background listeners synchronously and assume the worker/event page can be suspended.
5. Request permissions only when the user invokes the feature, explain the benefit and preserve reduced functionality after denial or revocation.
6. Package all executable logic locally and enforce a restrictive Manifest V3 content security policy.
7. Verify each declared browser and surface; document real differences and fallbacks instead of claiming false parity.

## Phase 0 — Route browser and surface

Read [extension surfaces](references/extension-surfaces.md) and [browser compatibility](references/browser-compatibility.md). Determine:

- Chromium, Firefox and Safari targets plus minimum versions;
- popup, side panel/sidebar, options/onboarding, overlay, new-tab and DevTools surfaces actually needed;
- state ownership, data sensitivity and network boundaries;
- required versus optional API/host/data-collection permissions;
- fallback surface for unsupported APIs.

Use capability detection rather than user-agent sniffing. Keep separate static manifest outputs when browser keys or background implementations differ.

## Phase 1 — Define the privileged interaction

Record the current-tab context, user goal, primary action, data read/changed, trust boundaries, permission rationale, persistence requirement, failure/revocation path and store disclosure.

For each surface, define its open/close lifecycle, focus entry/return, width classes, keyboard path, empty/loading/offline/denied/revoked/error states and handoff to a more durable surface.

## Phase 2 — Establish visual grammar and themes

Read [style recipes](references/style-recipes.md). Adapt one recipe to a constrained browser surface; use dense styling only when labels and targets remain usable. Read [style packs](references/style-packs.md) when the brief calls for expressive reference-derived directions (aurora focus, neon arena, graphite glass, pastel glass, vivid tiles, playful gradient); apply their brand primitives from `assets/theme-packs.css` via `data-brand` without touching semantic roles. When the brief names a product idea, open [product blueprints](references/product-blueprints.md) first — `assets/blueprints.json` seeds recipe, pack, components, data grammar and first states for fifty common products, and its derivation procedure covers every other idea.

Read [theme system](references/theme-system.md). Support system, light and dark modes; add OLED when valuable. Apply stored choice from an external CSP-safe module, use local fonts/icons and validate forced colors and reduced motion. Do not depend on deprecated browser-provided extension styling.

## Phase 3 — Compose from extension contracts

Read [component contracts](references/component-contracts.md), then inspect `assets/component-contracts.json`. For glow, gradient, glass, ring, tile and loader elements, read [advanced elements](references/advanced-elements.md) and compose from `assets/advanced-ui.css`; adapt community elements (uiverse and similar) only through its hardening checklist. Optional interactive polish (spotlight, tilt, count-up, tab keyboarding, toasts, dialogs with focus return, carousel dots, compare sliders, copy buttons, ticker pause) comes from `assets/ifx-behaviors.js` and must degrade cleanly when absent. When the brief asks for scrolling effects, 3D product motion, exploded views or cinematic story pages, read [3D product scrollytelling](references/scrollytelling-3d.md) — its section 0 adapts the contract to this surface — pick one recipe from `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json` and drive it with `assets/scroll-scene.js`. Every element must define surface fit, minimum size, data, lifecycle-safe interactions, accessibility, theme behavior, responsive adaptation, states and misuse.

Popup rule: show current status/context, one primary action and a route to detail. Side panel/sidebar rule: support persistent contextual multi-step work. Options rule: expose durable preferences, privacy, permission scope, export/reset and account controls. Overlay rule: isolate from the host page, avoid obstruction and always provide explicit dismissal.

## Phase 4 — Implement state and messaging

Read [state and messaging](references/extension-state-messaging.md).

- Store durable state with the extension storage API or established persistence layer; never rely on global/background/popup memory.
- Use discriminated message types, validate payloads and verify sender/tab/origin where relevant.
- Return structured success/error responses; never render message-provided markup.
- Keep long operations in the background context or a durable page and let transient surfaces reconnect.
- Feature-detect `globalThis.browser ?? globalThis.chrome` methods and provide per-browser fallbacks.
- Use alarms/events rather than `setInterval` for background scheduling.

## Phase 5 — Enforce security and permission discipline

Read [extension security](references/extension-security.md) before editing manifests, content scripts, messages or network code. Use `assets/extension-starter/` as a conservative reference.

Use `assets/browser-api.js` and `assets/extension-storage.js` as small capability/persistence adapters, and `assets/extension-shell.css` for constrained container behavior. In this skill package or repository, run `node scripts/audit-extension.mjs <built-extension-root>` before delivery; allow a nonstarter permission only through an explicit reviewed `--allow-permission` argument.

Reject remotely hosted scripts, inline handlers/scripts, evaluated strings, wildcard default host access, broad web-accessible resources, unsafe HTML sinks and message-controlled arbitrary URLs. Prefer `activeTab` and optional specific host permissions when the task permits.

## Phase 6 — Verify

Read [extension quality gates](references/extension-quality-gates.md) and [visual QA](references/visual-qa.md). At minimum:

- load/test each manifest target and surface;
- verify popup closure/reopen, worker suspension, browser restart and state restoration;
- test denied/revoked permissions, restricted pages, offline/stale data and signed-out state;
- keyboard-test entry, focus order, dialogs, dismissal and handoffs;
- test micro, compact, regular and wide container widths plus 200% zoom;
- verify system/light/dark/forced-colors and reduced-motion behavior;
- audit CSP, local executable assets, permissions, web-accessible resources and message boundaries;
- inspect console/runtime errors and package contents.

## Delivery standard

Report supported browsers/surfaces, manifest differences, required and optional permissions with rationale, checks actually run and any store/platform limitation. Never claim cross-browser support from manifest parsing alone.

## Reference map

| Need | Read |
|---|---|
| Surface selection and sizing | `references/extension-surfaces.md` |
| State, worker lifecycle and messages | `references/extension-state-messaging.md` |
| CSP, permissions, trust and safe rendering | `references/extension-security.md` |
| Chromium, Firefox and Safari differences | `references/browser-compatibility.md` |
| Extension-specific QA | `references/extension-quality-gates.md` |
| Element behavior contracts | `references/component-contracts.md` + `assets/component-contracts.json` |
| Visual direction and themes | `references/style-recipes.md`, `references/theme-system.md` |
| Reference-derived packs and brand primitives | `references/style-packs.md` + `assets/theme-packs.css` |
| Expressive elements (glow, glass, rings, tiles) | `references/advanced-elements.md` + `assets/advanced-ui.css` |
| Blueprint for any product idea | `references/product-blueprints.md` + `assets/blueprints.json` |
| 3D product scrollytelling and exploded views | `references/scrollytelling-3d.md` + `references/scrollytelling-references.md` + `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json` + `assets/scroll-scene.js` |
| Capability, storage and extension-safe starter assets | `assets/browser-api.js`, `assets/extension-storage.js`, `assets/extension-shell.css`, `assets/extension-starter/` |
| Deterministic MV3/CSP/permission audit | `scripts/audit-extension.mjs` |

# Browser compatibility

Generate separate static manifests from one reviewed capability model when keys differ.

## Chromium

- Use `action`, `background.service_worker`, `side_panel`/`chrome.sidePanel`, `options_ui`, `chrome_url_overrides` and `devtools_page` as required.
- Service workers have no DOM and can suspend; persist state and register listeners synchronously.
- A side panel needs an options/popup/tab fallback when other targets are supported.

## Firefox

- Use `action` and `sidebar_action`/`browser.sidebarAction` for the sidebar surface.
- Firefox Manifest V3 currently uses background scripts/event pages rather than `background.service_worker`; a cross-browser manifest can declare both, but separate outputs are easier to audit.
- Do not depend on deprecated `browser_style` in Manifest V3.
- Signing requires a Gecko extension id, and new submissions require `browser_specific_settings.gecko.data_collection_permissions`, including `required: ["none"]` when no listed data is transmitted.

## Safari

- Safari Web Extensions require Xcode packaging/distribution and may communicate with a containing native app.
- Feature-detect APIs because unsupported manifest keys can be ignored.
- Do not assume `storage.sync` synchronizes or that identity and blocking request APIs match Chromium.
- Provide popup/options/native handoff fallbacks for unsupported side-panel behavior.
- Test macOS and iOS/iPadOS surfaces separately when both are claimed.

## Shared rule

`globalThis.browser ?? globalThis.chrome` is only a namespace starting point. Detect each method, permissions model and promise/callback behavior. Maintain a support matrix with verified browser versions and fallbacks.

The packaged adapters assume Promise-capable Manifest V3 API forms in the product's declared current Chromium and Firefox baselines. If a baseline includes callback-only versions, wrap only the affected methods with reviewed method-specific adapters and test them; never make a generic helper invoke an API twice.

# Style recipe matrix

Choose a coherent recipe from product context and audience. A recipe is a design grammar, not a preset skin. Combine at most two recipes and state which rules come from each.

## Contents

1. Selection axes
2. Recipe matrix
3. Compatibility
4. Reference-image translation

## 1. Selection axes

Decide these axes before choosing visual effects:

- **Trust:** institutional ↔ experimental
- **Density:** compact ↔ spacious
- **Tempo:** calm ↔ urgent
- **Surface:** flat ↔ layered ↔ translucent
- **Geometry:** precise ↔ soft ↔ expressive
- **Data ink:** restrained ↔ saturated
- **Motion:** still ↔ feedback-led ↔ narrative

## 2. Recipe matrix

| Recipe | Composition | Type and geometry | Color/surface | Data visualization | Motion | Avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Executive | Stable grid, strong summary row, progressive disclosure | Neutral grotesk, medium radius, disciplined alignment | Quiet neutrals, one authoritative accent, solid elevation | Direct labels, restrained categorical palette, variance and forecast emphasis | Short feedback and subtle crossfades | Decorative gradients, unexplained gauges, novelty navigation |
| Finance | Dense comparison, persistent filters, audit-friendly detail | Tabular numerals, compact controls, crisp separators | Neutral canvas, semantic positive/negative colors that remain distinguishable without hue | Candles/lines/bars/tables selected by question; show units, latency and source | Fast state transitions; no ambient motion | Green/red-only meaning, hidden fees, misleading truncated axes |
| Healthcare | Calm hierarchy, patient/task context always visible | Highly legible type, generous targets, soft but clear geometry | Low-chroma surfaces, trustworthy status colors, strong focus | Ranges, thresholds and uncertainty; never imply diagnosis from decoration | Gentle feedback, reduced motion by default for sensitive flows | Alarm fatigue, low-contrast pastels, unsupported medical claims |
| Cyber | Operational density, incident priority, evidence/detail split | Compact mono only for identifiers/code, firm geometry | Dark or light neutral base with sparse high-salience status | Timelines, topology, severity distribution, event tables | Purposeful alerts and trace transitions | Neon everywhere, movie-terminal clichés, color-only severity |
| Creator | Content-forward canvas, modular tools and preview | Expressive display face paired with readable UI sans, rounded modules | Brand-forward accents, editorial surfaces, selective gradients | Audience/content performance with annotated milestones | Responsive previews and tactile microinteractions | Controls competing with work, trend collage, excessive chrome |
| Gaming | Immersive media, strong progression and inventory hierarchy | Characterful headings, durable UI type, angular or sculpted cards | Dark/saturated worlds, tokenized rarity and state colors | Progression, performance, inventory and comparison with redundant labels | Energetic but interruptible; respect reduced motion | Illegible sci-fi fonts, glow on all text, manipulative reward loops |
| Calm | Breathing room, one task per region, progressive detail | Humanist type, soft geometry, generous line height | Low-stimulation neutrals and one soft accent; light/dark parity | Minimal charts with direct labels and humane time scales | Slow optional transitions, no perpetual attention loops | Washed-out contrast, hidden actions, empty decorative space |
| Editorial | Strong narrative grid, art direction and typographic contrast | Display/editorial face plus restrained UI sans, asymmetric rhythm | Content-led palette, large fields of neutral color | Annotated figures embedded in narrative | Section reveals and media transitions that preserve reading | Template-like bento repetition, excessive card borders |
| Developer tooling | Workspace shell, keyboard-first commands, code/output separation | UI sans plus mono for code/data only, tight predictable geometry | Neutral surfaces, semantic syntax/status tokens, optional dark-first mode | Logs, traces, tables, flame/timeline patterns with filters | Instant command feedback, no ornamental latency | Fake terminal styling, unreadable dense panes, mouse-only commands |

## 3. Compatibility

Compatible combinations include Executive + Finance, Healthcare + Calm, Cyber + Developer tooling, Creator + Editorial and Gaming + Creator. If combining recipes, retain one composition system and one type scale; borrow only a secondary surface or motion language.

Do not combine glass, neo-skeuomorphism, brutalism, maximal gradients and spatial 3D merely because each appears in a reference set.

## 4. Reference-image translation

Translate reference collections into reusable principles:

- Compact rings, gauges and sparklines imply **telemetry grammar**: value + unit + timeframe + threshold + trend.
- Mixed-size analytics cards imply **bento hierarchy**: grid spans reflect decision importance, not random visual variety.
- Translucent pastel panels imply **layer grammar**: blur is limited, text remains on sufficiently opaque surfaces and light/dark modes are independently tuned.
- Dark mobile concepts imply **focus grammar**: one luminous action/metric, quieter supporting surfaces and explicit OLED-safe blacks where desired.
- Extension concepts imply **constraint grammar**: immediate status, one primary action, persistent state outside the popup and clear permission boundaries.

Never copy logos, character art, proprietary content or a full composition from a visual reference.

# Style packs

Reference-derived visual directions distilled into reusable principles. Each pack extends a base recipe from `style-recipes.md`, ships brand primitives in `assets/theme-packs.css` (`data-brand`), and leans on specific elements from `references/advanced-elements.md`. Packs translate reference imagery into grammar — palette behavior, geometry, glow budget, telemetry treatment. Never copy a reference composition, illustration, character, logo or copy.

Activate a pack by setting `data-brand` on the root alongside `data-theme`. Packs override brand primitives only; every component keeps consuming semantic roles.

## Pack matrix

| Pack | Base recipe | Default scheme | Palette behavior | Geometry & surface | Signature elements | Avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `aurora` | Calm + Gaming focus grammar | dark / OLED | Deep space navy canvas; one luminous indigo-violet accent; cool cyan/violet support; glow reserved for the focus object | Large radii, deep layered surfaces, radial ambience behind a single hero | Glow ring for the active session, `ifx-btn--glow` primary, `ifx-orb` ambience, gradient stat bars | Glow on body text; more than one luminous center; neon rainbow drift |
| `neon-arena` | Gaming + Creator | dark | Charcoal neutrals; spring-green signal accent for live/primary only; media supplies the color | Rounded cards, pill chips, circular FAB-like accents | `ifx-live` viewer badges, `ifx-chip` filter rows, green `ifx-btn--glow`, chat list density | Green as a series color for data; accent-colored long text; glow on every thumbnail |
| `graphite-glass` | Gaming + Editorial commerce | dark | Warm graphite glass; cyan-teal accent; artwork carries saturation | Soft glass panels over media, gentle inner light, generous card radii | `ifx-card-glass` over renders, cyan `ifx-btn--gradient` buy action, rating rows with numeric value | Copying character art; glass under small text; teal-on-graphite below 4.5:1 |
| `pastel-glass` | Calm + Creator | light | Lavender/pink/peach wash; violet action; mint success; low-chroma ink | Frosted translucent cards, big radii, airy spacing, soft colored shadows | `ifx-card-glass` clusters, pastel rings, `ifx-switch` gradient-on, gentle `ifx-orb` wash | Washed-out contrast; blur under paragraphs; pastel status colors that lose meaning |
| `vivid-tiles` | Executive telemetry, consumer tone | light or OLED | Quiet shell; saturated one-hue-per-tile gradients; ink locked to contrast per tile | Extra-round 24px tiles, oversized numerals, day columns | `ifx-tile` bento, `ifx-daystrip`, mini `ifx-ring--xs` per day, explicit skip cells | Two metrics per tile; lime/yellow tiles with white ink; decorative emoji replacing state text |
| `playful-grad` | Creator consumer | light | Purple-to-mint brand gradient; white cards on lilac canvas; mint reserved for success/CTA pair | Pill-heavy geometry, chunky controls, friendly 3D-ish icon slots | `ifx-btn--gradient`, `ifx-progress` gradient fill, gradient-border feature card | Gradient text; icon clutter; mint and purple fighting for the same job |

## Cross-pack grammars

**Widget telemetry (from vivid widget references).** A glanceable tile answers one question: headline value + unit, goal or comparison in words ("7,278 of 8,000 steps"), a 4–7 day strip with per-day values, and explicit skip/missing markers. Trend direction appears in text, not only arrow color. Minimum tile 160×96 CSS px; below that, drop the micro-chart before the words.

**Complication grammar (from watch-face references).** A complication is the smallest honest datum: one value, one unit or symbol, one bounded ring/arc, optional threshold ticks. Type floor 11px equivalent; tappable complications keep a 44px hit area even when drawn smaller; color never carries the only meaning — position and text do.

**Focus-session grammar (from the quiet-mode reference).** A focus screen has exactly one luminous object: the countdown ring with exact remaining time centered, muted context chips (allowed people, silenced count, next block) and a single end/extend action pair. Time renders from a monotonic end-time source; everything else dims rather than competes.

**Ethereal hero grammar (from the clinical 3D-hero reference).** One centered 3D or illustrated hero may anchor a light glass dashboard; data callouts connect to it as labeled chips with leader lines, each repeating its value in plain text. The hero never replaces the data layer: every callout metric also exists in an ordinary card or table, and the whole scene collapses to a stacked list on narrow widths and under reduced motion.

## Choosing and combining

Pick one pack per product. A pack may borrow one grammar from another (e.g., `aurora` + widget telemetry for its stats route) but never a second palette. If none fits, fall back to the base recipe matrix and derive fresh brand primitives — a pack is a shortcut, not a ceiling.

## Derived packs (v2 — principle-built, no reference imagery)

| Pack | Default scheme | Character | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sunset-pop` | light | Coral-to-pink warmth, bold friendly type | Marketing, creator tools, consumer launches |
| `forest-calm` | light | Natural greens, airy spacing | Wellness, sustainability, outdoors, finance-with-calm |
| `mono-brutal` | light | Monochrome, sharp edges, zero decorative motion | Portfolios, editorial, docs, brutalist briefs |
| `terminal-dev` | dark | Phosphor green on graphite, monospace-forward | Consoles, CI, API tooling, on-call surfaces |
| `royal-lux` | dark | Gold-as-jewelry over deep navy | Premium commerce, private banking, ticketing VIP |
| `clinical-care` | light | Trustworthy blue, unambiguous status | Patient portals, telehealth, HR and civic services |

Same law as v1 packs: brand primitives only, one pack per product, forced-colors defers to system colors.

## Derived packs (v3)

| Pack | Default scheme | Character | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `paper-ink` | light | Warm paper neutrals, ink hierarchy, one brick accent | Editorial, docs, case studies, long-form reading |
| `slate-pro` | light | Disciplined slate grays with one confident blue | B2B admin, enterprise consoles, workhorse SaaS |

# Theme system

Build themes from semantic roles and independent axes. A dark theme is not an inverted light theme.

## Contents

1. Theme axes
2. Required tokens
3. Resolution and persistence
4. Data visualization
5. Accessibility
6. Validation

## 1. Theme axes

Model theme selection as independent attributes:

| Axis | Values | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Mode | system, light, dark, oled | Luminance preference and platform context |
| Contrast | standard, high, forced-colors | Perception and OS accessibility |
| Density | compact, comfortable, spacious | Information and control spacing |
| Surface | solid, elevated, translucent | Layer treatment |
| Geometry | precise, soft, pill-accented, expressive | Shape and boundary behavior |
| Recipe/brand | nine recipe directions plus product-specific primitives | Composition, hue, type and expressive character |
| Data palette | categorical, sequential, diverging, status | Analytical encoding policy |
| Motion | none, reduced, restrained, expressive | User preference, narrative need and device capability |

Use attributes such as `data-theme`, `data-density` and `data-surface`; avoid encoding all axes in one theme name.

## 2. Required tokens

Define at least:

- canvas, surface, surface-raised, surface-sunken and overlay backgrounds;
- primary, secondary, muted, inverse and disabled text;
- subtle, default and strong borders plus focus ring;
- primary action and hover/pressed/disabled states;
- success, warning, danger and info backgrounds/text/borders;
- selection, link, visited-link and drag/drop indicators;
- shadow color/opacity and overlay scrim;
- chart foreground, grid, axis, tooltip, positive/negative and categorical/sequential/diverging palettes.

Components consume semantic tokens only. Brand primitives may exist privately, but application components must not depend on raw palette names such as `blue-500`.

## 3. Resolution and persistence

Resolve mode in this order:

1. forced-colors/high-contrast platform behavior;
2. explicit user choice;
3. authenticated profile or tenant setting;
4. `prefers-color-scheme`;
5. documented product default.

Apply the resolved mode before first paint. Load the local, synchronous `assets/theme-bootstrap.js` in the document head before theme CSS, then initialize `assets/theme-controller.js` for switching, validated persistence, system changes and same-origin tab synchronization. Both files are dependency-free; adapt the storage layer when local storage is not the product's source of truth.

Set `color-scheme: light dark` so form controls and browser UI follow the active mode. Do not store a forced theme when the user selects System.

## 4. Data visualization

- Define chart colors separately for every mode; do not rely on opacity over an unknown surface.
- Keep series identity stable across routes and modes where possible.
- Provide shapes, strokes, labels or patterns when color carries meaning.
- Use sequential palettes for magnitude, diverging palettes around a meaningful midpoint and categorical palettes for unordered series.
- Reserve status colors for status; do not reuse danger red as an ordinary series color.
- Keep grid/axis contrast sufficient to orient without competing with data.

## 5. Accessibility

- Body text and essential labels target at least 4.5:1; large text targets at least 3:1.
- Focus and meaningful non-text boundaries target at least 3:1 against adjacent colors.
- Muted text remains readable; opacity alone must not create disabled state.
- Translucent surfaces require an opaque readability layer or tested worst-case backdrop.
- OLED mode uses near-black raised surfaces to preserve hierarchy; avoid large full-white fields.
- Forced-colors mode keeps content and controls operable with system colors.
- Theme switching must not reset focus, scroll, filters or unsaved work.

## 6. Validation

For every mode and brand combination:

1. validate required token presence;
2. compute declared text/action/status contrast pairs;
3. inspect charts and screenshots on representative routes;
4. test native controls, autofill, selection, focus and disabled states;
5. test 200% zoom, reduced motion and forced colors;
6. test first paint and persistence without a mode flash.

# Product blueprints

Sixty starting points that make the skill work for any product idea. Each blueprint maps an idea to the decisions the workflow needs: core user question, recipe, brand pack, per-surface shape, a starting bill of materials (`assets/component-contracts.json` ids), expressive elements (`assets/advanced-ui.css` classes), the data grammar that keeps it honest, the states to design first, and the pitfalls that sink that product category. The machine-readable catalog is `assets/blueprints.json`.

## How to use a blueprint

1. **Match** the brief to a blueprint by its core question, not its title — a "plant watering app" is `habit-tracker` wearing leaves.
2. **Adapt, don't obey**: the recipe and pack are defaults. Swap the pack freely (one pack per product); swap the recipe only with a reason.
3. **Bill of materials**: components listed are the minimum interesting set; every one still owes its full contract states.
4. **States first**: build the `firstStates` before polishing the happy path — they are where this category earns or loses trust.
5. **Mashups**: combine at most two blueprints by taking the primary's recipe + pack and borrowing the secondary's grammar (e.g., `crm-sales` + `ai-copilot` = pipeline with an agent pane that logs its actions).

## When no blueprint matches — derivation procedure

1. Write the **core question** the person asks the screen (one sentence, their words).
2. Name the **primary loop**: capture, monitor, decide, browse, communicate, create, or operate. That picks the hero surface (form, dashboard, queue, gallery, thread, canvas, console).
3. Pick the **recipe** from the matrix by tempo and density; pick a **pack** or derive brand primitives; state the one-glow budget.
4. Choose components from the contract catalog to answer the core question **above the fold**; everything else is progressive disclosure.
5. Write the **data grammar** line (value + unit + window + baseline + freshness for anything numeric) and the four ugliest states; design those first.

A derived product that follows this procedure is a valid blueprint — consider contributing it back into `assets/blueprints.json`.

# Extension surfaces

Choose the surface from task duration, persistence and required space.

## Contents

1. Surface matrix
2. Width classes
3. Entry and handoff
4. Surface-specific rules

## 1. Surface matrix

| Surface | Best for | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Action popup | Current-page status and one quick action | Long work, deep navigation, volatile unsaved state |
| Chrome side panel / Firefox sidebar | Persistent contextual workflows beside a page | Assuming the APIs/manifests are compatible |
| Options page | Durable settings, privacy, account, data export/reset | Frequent in-context actions |
| Onboarding page | Value explanation, sign-in and staged permission setup | Requesting every permission before value |
| Content overlay | Direct annotation or control tied to page content | Blocking host controls, unsafe host styling/content |
| New-tab page | Fast keyboard-first daily workspace | Deceptive browser chrome or slow mandatory network load |
| DevTools panel | Inspection, logs, network/data tooling | General consumer workflows |
| Toolbar badge/icon | Very short status or entry point | Encoding detailed meaning or using color alone |

## 2. Width classes

Use container queries and intrinsic layout:

- **micro:** below 280px—status, label and one action only;
- **compact:** 280–359px—single-column popup or narrow sidebar;
- **regular:** 360–479px—richer popup/sidebar with grouped detail;
- **wide:** 480px and above—side panel, options, new-tab or DevTools layouts.

Do not force popup dimensions that overflow the browser. Keep popup content one column, scrollable when necessary and useful at 200% zoom.

## 3. Entry and handoff

Every transient surface must have a durable handoff: open side panel, options or a tab for tasks that exceed the popup. Preserve context through storage or a short-lived token, not a global variable.

Show which tab/site/account the action affects. When context is unavailable or restricted, explain why and offer only safe alternatives.

## 4. Surface-specific rules

### Popup

- Render immediately from cached state, then refresh.
- Keep one primary action and no more than two navigation levels.
- Persist every meaningful mutation before the popup can close.
- Do not display a success state that depends on the popup remaining open.

### Side panel/sidebar

- Support resizable width and tab/window context changes.
- Show whether state follows the active tab, is pinned, or is global.
- Preserve drafts and selection across tab navigation.

### Options/onboarding

- Separate required, optional and site-specific permissions.
- Show current permission status from the API rather than optimistic UI state.
- Include privacy/data-collection, export and reset behavior where relevant.

### Content overlay

- Treat the host DOM/CSS as hostile; use Shadow DOM or strict namespace/isolation.
- Bound z-index and placement, avoid covering browser/page-critical controls, and reposition on viewport changes.
- Provide visible close plus Escape and restore host focus/selection.

### DevTools/new tab

- DevTools panes must handle resizing, detached targets and high-volume data without blocking.
- New-tab surfaces must initialize fast, work offline where promised and never imitate trusted browser chrome.

# Advanced elements

Expressive elements — glow, gradients, glass, rings, tiles, loaders — in the spirit of community element libraries (uiverse.io, css-loaders and similar), rebuilt on Interface Forge semantic tokens. The implementation is `assets/advanced-ui.css` (`ifx-` prefix); brand color sources are `assets/theme-packs.css`. These elements are seasoning, not structure: they never replace the component contracts in `assets/component-contracts.json`, and every element here still owes complete states, keyboard behavior and honest data.

## Contents

1. Budget rules
2. Element catalog
3. Telemetry grammar for expressive gauges
4. Adapting community elements (uiverse and similar)
5. Guardrails reference

## 1. Budget rules

- **One glow center per view.** `ifx-btn--glow`, `ifx-ring--glow` and `ifx-live` compete for the same attention; pick the element that carries the primary action or the live truth, and keep everything else quiet.
- **At most one gradient direction per screen.** `--ifx-grad-a/b` define it; reusing the pair across button, ring and card border is coherence, mixing new hues per element is noise.
- **Glass is a layer treatment, not a theme.** Two glass depths maximum; body text always sits on a surface at `--ifx-glass-opacity` or higher (see theme-system.md §5).
- **Neumorphism only on calm, low-density surfaces** with real borders retained; never for status or destructive actions, where soft shadows read as disabled.
- **Vivid tiles carry one metric each.** Tile ink must pass 4.5:1 on both gradient stops; the lime/yellow family requires the dark ink override (`--ifx-tile3-ink` pattern).
- Decorative ambience (`ifx-orb`, aurora backdrops) is `aria-hidden`, sits behind content, never animates under reduced motion, and never reduces text contrast below target.

## 2. Element catalog

| Element | Class | Use for | Never for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glow button | `ifx-btn ifx-btn--glow` | The single primary action in luminous dark directions | Rows of actions; destructive actions |
| Gradient button | `ifx-btn ifx-btn--gradient` | Brand-forward primary CTA on marketing surfaces | Dense product toolbars |
| Gradient-border button | `ifx-btn ifx-btn--border-gradient` | Secondary emphasis beside a filled primary | Being the only affordance signal |
| Shine sweep | `+ ifx-btn--shine` | One hero CTA hover flourish | Anything that loops or plays on load |
| Soft/neumorphic button | `ifx-btn ifx-btn--soft` | Quiet controls in calm recipes | Status, danger, or low-contrast themes |
| Animated switch | `input.ifx-switch` | Boolean settings with immediate effect | Actions that need confirmation |
| Checkbox / radio | `.ifx-check`, `.ifx-radio` | Forms and option groups | Replacing native semantics |
| Filter chip | `.ifx-chip` (`aria-pressed`) | Toggleable filters and categories | Navigation between routes |
| Live badge | `.ifx-live` | Genuinely live/realtime state with viewer or event count in text | Decorating static content |
| Glass card | `.ifx-card-glass` | Layered panels over rich or media backdrops | Long-form reading surfaces |
| Gradient-border card | `.ifx-card-border-gradient` | One featured/reward/highlight card per view | Every card in a grid |
| Neumorphic card | `.ifx-card-neu` | Calm widgets on pale canvases | Dark-first or high-contrast products |
| Vivid tile | `.ifx-tile` (+ `--ifx-tile-a/b/-ink`) | Glanceable single-metric bento/widget cards | Multi-metric dashboards, tiny text |
| Progress ring | `.ifx-ring` (`--val`) | Progress toward a known goal, exact value centered | Unbounded metrics; angle-only meaning |
| Gradient/glow ring | `+ --gradient` / `--glow` | The one hero metric of a focus screen | Grids of rings |
| Arc gauge | `.ifx-arc` | Bounded physical/operational ranges | Precise comparison (use bars/table) |
| Segmented meter | `.ifx-segmeter--clip` | Discrete progress (sets, steps, quota) | Continuous fine-grained values |
| Day strip | `.ifx-daystrip` | 4–7 day habit/metric recap with per-day value text | More than 7 columns; hover-only values |
| Complication | `.ifx-complication` | Micro circular datum in dense rows/watch-like surfaces | Anything tappable below 44px, text below 11px |
| Spinner / dots | `.ifx-spinner`, `.ifx-dots` | Short indeterminate waits with an accessible busy label | Waits over ~3s (show progress or skeleton) |
| Shimmer skeleton | `.ifx-shimmer` | Predictable-geometry loading placeholders | Unknown layouts; masking errors |
| Progress bar | `.ifx-progress` (`--val`) | Determinate progress with value in text | Fake/optimistic progress |
| Tooltip | `.ifx-tip[data-tip]` | Supplementary hints on hover **and** focus | The only path to a label or value |
| Ambient orbs | `.ifx-orb` | Depth behind heroes in aurora/pastel directions | Behind data visualizations |

## 3. Telemetry grammar for expressive gauges

Rings, arcs, meters, tiles, day strips and complications remain bound by the metric grammar: exact value, unit, timeframe, comparison/threshold meaning and freshness expressed **in text**, never only by angle, fill or hue. Set `--val` from data, mirror it in the centered value, and give the element a text alternative (`role="img"` + label, or adjacent text) that a screen reader can consume. A skipped day in a day strip is rendered as an explicit skip cell, not an empty gap.

## 4. Adapting community elements (uiverse and similar)

Community galleries are a legitimate source of interaction ideas. Before shipping an adapted element, run this checklist:

1. **License** — confirm the snippet's license (uiverse is MIT) and keep any required attribution in source comments; never copy branded or trademarked artwork.
2. **Tokenize** — replace every literal color with a semantic `--if-*` or expressive `--ifx-*` token; no raw hex may survive in component CSS.
3. **Real elements** — rebuild `div`-buttons and `span`-checkboxes on `button`, `input`, `a`; keep native semantics and labels.
4. **Focus** — add `:focus-visible` treatment at ≥3:1 contrast; remove any `outline: none` without replacement.
5. **Hit size** — enforce `--if-control-min` (44px coarse-pointer) even when the visual is smaller, via padding or pseudo-element hit area.
6. **Motion** — gate loops, sweeps, pulses and parallax behind `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`; hover flourishes must also fire on focus.
7. **Forced colors** — verify Windows High Contrast: replace glow/gradient meaning with borders and system colors (`ButtonBorder`, `Highlight`).
8. **Contrast** — check text on gradients at **both** stops and on glass over the worst-case backdrop; adjust ink or opacity floor, not the claim.
9. **States** — add hover, active, disabled, busy and error treatments; a pretty default state alone is not shippable.
10. **Weight** - prefer CSS-only; if a snippet needs JS, keep it dependency-free and idempotent.

An element that cannot pass 3–8 is a decoration, not a component — drop it or redesign it.

## 5. Guardrails reference

`assets/advanced-ui.css` already encodes: reduced-motion removal of all loops and sweeps; reduced-transparency solid fallback for glass; forced-colors fallbacks for every element; focus-visible rings from `--if-focus`; tabular numerals on all value slots. When extending the library, extend these guard blocks in the same commit — an element without its guardrails does not merge.

## 6. v2 element additions

Forms: `ifx-field` + `ifx-input`, floating label `ifx-float`, `ifx-search`, `ifx-otp`, `ifx-slider`, `ifx-stepper`, star `ifx-rating` (real radios, DOM 5→1 with row-reverse), drop zone `ifx-file`.
Navigation: `ifx-tabs` (pair with `ifx-behaviors.js` for arrow keys), segmented `ifx-seg` (radios + `:has`), `ifx-breadcrumb`, `ifx-steps`, `ifx-fab`, `ifx-dock` (safe-area aware), `ifx-pagination`, `ifx-menu`.
Data display: `ifx-avatar`/`ifx-avatar-stack`, `ifx-badge`, `ifx-status`, `ifx-kbd`, `ifx-timeline`, `ifx-accordion` (native details), `ifx-table` in `ifx-table-wrap`, `ifx-stat` + `ifx-delta`, `ifx-heatgrid`, `ifx-bullet`, `ifx-legend`, `ifx-code`, `ifx-price`.
Feedback: `ifx-banner--info|success|warning|danger`, `ifx-toast` (+ `window.ifxToast`), `ifx-empty`.
Effects: `ifx-text-grad` (display headlines ≥ 28px only, both stops pass contrast), `ifx-divider-glow`, `ifx-bg-grid`/`ifx-bg-dots`, `ifx-spotlight` and `ifx-tilt` (decorative, fine-pointer, via `data-ifx`), `ifx-beam` (one per view; stills under reduced motion), `ifx-count` (via `data-ifx-count`).

Additional budget rules: heat grids always pair with per-cell text values and a numeric legend; `ifx-seg` switches views of one object while `ifx-tabs` switches content panels; the toast region is a polite live region — errors that need decisions get a banner or dialog instead; `ifx-behaviors.js` is optional progressive enhancement — every element must remain fully usable without it.

## 7. v3 element additions

Overlays: `ifx-modal`, `ifx-drawer`, `ifx-sheet` (all on native `<dialog>`, wired by `ifx-behaviors.js` via `data-ifx-open`/`data-ifx-close` with focus return), `ifx-popover` for `[popover]`.
Media & marketing: `ifx-carousel` + `ifx-carousel-dots` (scroll-snap, behaviors sync the dots), `ifx-compare` before/after (the range input is the real control), `ifx-ticker` (must ship with a pause control via `data-ifx-ticker-toggle`; static wrapped list under reduced motion), `ifx-testimonial`, `ifx-logo-row`, frames `ifx-window` / `ifx-phone` / `ifx-terminal` (chrome is decorative and aria-hidden; terminal commands pair with `data-ifx-copy` buttons).
Structure: `ifx-tree` (details-based), `ifx-calendar`, `ifx-chat-thread` + `ifx-chat-msg--in|--out`, `ifx-upload-item`, `ifx-notification`, `ifx-toolbar` + `ifx-icon-btn`, `ifx-diff`, `ifx-scroll-rail` (shared with scrollytelling landmarks), `ifx-skeleton-card`.

v3 budget rules: one ticker per page and never for critical information; carousels never autoplay; compare sliders label both sides on-surface and state the difference in text; frames never imitate interactive OS chrome; dialogs stack never.

# Extension security

Extension UI executes with privileges ordinary pages do not have. Minimize authority and treat every external value as untrusted.

## Contents

1. Manifest and CSP
2. Permissions
3. Rendering and injection
4. Messages and network
5. Exposure and privacy

## 1. Manifest and CSP

- Use Manifest V3.
- Package executable JavaScript, WebAssembly and styles locally.
- Require an extension-page CSP at least as strict as `script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'` and restrict default/worker/style/connect/image sources to the minimum.
- Never use `unsafe-eval`, `unsafe-inline`, evaluated strings, remote script imports or remote-injected script elements.
- Avoid sandbox pages unless the isolated capability has a documented reason and message boundary.

## 2. Permissions

- Start with no host permissions.
- Prefer `activeTab` for a user-invoked current-tab action.
- Put site-specific hosts and optional APIs in optional permissions and request them from the triggering user gesture.
- Explain benefit, data read/changed, duration and fallback before requesting.
- Detect denial and revocation with the permissions API; never present an optimistic toggle as truth.
- High-risk permissions such as debugger, native messaging, proxy, management, cookies, history, browsing data or broad request interception require explicit product/security review and must not appear in a generic starter.

## 3. Rendering and injection

- Build DOM with `textContent`, attributes and created elements or a framework's escaped text path.
- Reject `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, unsafe template HTML and inline event attributes for untrusted data.
- Validate URLs and allow only intended schemes/origins before navigation or fetch.
- Isolate overlays from host styles and avoid reading more page content than the active feature needs.

## 4. Messages and network

- Validate message schema, sender and authorization.
- Never allow a message to select an arbitrary URL, script, host permission or privileged API method.
- Use HTTPS for remote data, exact allowlists and clear authentication/session expiry handling.
- Keep credentials/tokens out of DOM, logs and web-accessible resources.

## 5. Exposure and privacy

- Expose only exact required files through `web_accessible_resources`; never wildcard resources or matches.
- Avoid `externally_connectable` unless the external integration is essential and allowlisted.
- Disclose collected/transmitted data accurately for each store.
- Make reset/export/account deletion behavior match real storage and remote state.

# Extension quality gates

Before delivery:

1. Load every target manifest in the actual browser or document why unavailable.
2. Open popup, side panel/sidebar, options, onboarding, overlay, new-tab and DevTools surfaces included in scope.
3. Verify popup closes/reopens without losing meaningful state.
4. Exercise background suspension/restart and browser restart.
5. Exercise granted, denied and revoked permissions plus restricted/internal pages.
6. Verify no broad host permission is required before the feature that needs it.
7. Audit CSP, packaged scripts/styles, web-accessible resources and external connections.
8. Search for unsafe HTML/evaluation sinks and validate message sender/payload handling.
9. Test keyboard entry/order/dismissal, focus return and screen-reader names.
10. Test micro, compact, regular and wide containers, 200% zoom and long localized/RTL content.
11. Test system/light/dark, forced colors, reduced motion and reduced transparency.
12. Test offline, stale, signed-out, empty, partial, error and recovery states.
13. Inspect console errors, memory/CPU while idle and high-volume DevTools/side-panel data.
14. Inspect the final archive for only intended local files and verify manifest-referenced paths.

Store-readiness requires accurate permission/data disclosures, working privacy/support links when included, local executable code and screenshots/descriptions that match real behavior.

# 3D Product Scrollytelling — Exploded Assemblies & Cinematic Technical Visualization

Scroll-driven product storytelling: assembled → rotate → open → explode → focus → annotate → reassemble. This chapter owns **part-level product choreography** — exploded views, disassembly, cutaways, x-ray reveals — on the premium black-background aesthetic. It builds on [threejs-scroll-world.md](threejs-scroll-world.md) (scene architecture, R3F/vanilla wiring, lifecycle) and [motion-3d-playbook.md](motion-3d-playbook.md) (Lenis + GSAP ScrollTrigger setup); read those for the how, this for the what and the rules.

Machine-readable assets: `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json` (deterministic beat maps) and `assets/scroll-scene.js` (renderer-agnostic progress engine). Reference imagery and study links: [scrollytelling-references.md](scrollytelling-references.md).

## 0. Extension adaptation (read first on this skill)

Scrollytelling belongs **only on full-tab extension surfaces** — the onboarding page, a new-tab takeover, or a marketing/upgrade page. Never in the popup or side panel: those surfaces exist for status and one action, and their users arrived to configure, not to be sold. Deltas: total 3D payload ≤ 3 MB; pin ≤ 300vh; one focus beat maximum; the skip link is mandatory and appears within the first viewport; everything else in this chapter applies unchanged.

## Contents

1. When to reach for this (and when not)
2. The primitive: scroll progress owns the scene
3. Recipe catalog
4. Beat maps
5. Rendering tiers and the never-flatten rule
6. GLB and part conventions
7. The scroll engine contract
8. UX contract (non-negotiable)
9. Performance budgets
10. Accessibility and honest duplication

## 1. When to reach for this (and when not)

Reach for it when a **physical or physically-imagined product** is the hero and its internals or construction ARE the story: hardware launches (watch, phone, GPU, drone, camera, EV component, AI chip, robot), premium DTC objects (sneaker, espresso machine), technical credibility pages ("how it's built"), and configurators that earn a narrative intro. One scrollytelling scene per page; it is the landing's "one dominant motion idea" from [landing-system.md](landing-system.md), never an addition to one.

Do **not** use it for dashboards, tools, or any surface where the person came to act rather than be told a story; where no genuine part hierarchy exists (a T-shirt is not an assembly); or where the budget only affords a flattened video — then use an ordinary media section instead of a fake-interactive one.

## 2. The primitive: scroll progress owns the scene

Normalized progress `p ∈ [0,1]` over a pinned section is the **only clock**. Every scene property — camera distance/height/orbit/fov, per-part explosion, shell opacity, clip plane, highlight, caption — is a pure function of `p`. Consequences:

- **Scrub, never play.** No timers advance the scene. Scrolling back replays backward perfectly (reversibility is free when state is a function, impossible when it's a video you fired).
- **Deterministic beats.** A recipe is a list of keyframes (`beats`) at fixed `p` values; the engine interpolates numeric fields between adjacent beats and switches discrete fields at beat boundaries.
- The scene owns real objects (Tier A) whenever possible, so `p` can drive positions, materials, lights and annotations independently — the reason this beats scrubbing a video.

## 3. Recipe catalog

Twenty deterministic recipes ship in `assets/scrollytelling-recipes.json`. Pick **one primary** per scene; a second may be nested only as a sub-beat (e.g., `component-focus` inside `exploded-assembly` — the shipped `exploded-assembly` already includes two focus beats).

| Recipe | Intent | Tiers |
|---|---|---|
| `product-reveal` | Darkness → rim light → silhouette → full product | A B C |
| `exploded-assembly` | The canonical: rotate, explode, focus ×2, reassemble | A B |
| `product-disassembly` | Parts leave one by one in service order | A B |
| `internal-reveal` | Shell fades, internals stay lit | A B |
| `layer-peel` | Concentric layers lift in sequence (shoe, battery, PCB stack) | A B |
| `component-focus` | Camera dollies to one part; rest dims; spec appears | A B |
| `xray-reveal` | Materials go translucent by scroll; skeleton/frame glows | A |
| `material-transformation` | Raw material → machined → finished surface | A B C |
| `assembly-sequence` | Parts fly in and seat (reverse disassembly) | A B |
| `floating-components` | Parts drift in loose formation; labels attach | A |
| `orbital-inspection` | 360° orbit with 3–5 annotated stations | A B |
| `camera-fly-through` | Camera travels through the open product | A |
| `mechanical-operation` | One mechanism cycles as scroll advances (gears, hinge, shutter) | A B |
| `product-morph` | Model A transitions to model B (generations, sizes) | A |
| `cutaway-reveal` | Clip plane sweeps a cross-section | A |
| `particle-assembly` | Product condenses from particles, then solidifies | A |
| `technical-blueprint` | Wireframe/blueprint style resolves into rendered product | A |
| `reassembly-hero` | Exploded start; scroll assembles toward CTA | A B |
| `macro-zoom` | Extreme close-up travels the surface to a wide hero | A B C |
| `hero-to-grid` | Hero product recedes into a comparison/spec grid handoff | A B |

## 4. Beat maps

A beat map is the recipe's spine. Format (see the JSON for full schema):

```json
{ "p": 0.42, "label": "internals-emerge",
  "state": { "rotY": 0.35, "explode": 0.7, "shellFade": 0.85,
             "focus": -1, "camDist": 3.2, "camHeight": 0.4, "fov": 40 },
  "caption": "flight-controller" }
```

Worked ledger for `exploded-assembly` (the shipped default):

```
p 0.00  black; rim light only            0.52  full exploded state
  0.06  silhouette resolves              0.62  camera approaches board
  0.12  key light up, product assembled  0.70  board highlighted + spec caption
  0.20  slow quarter turn                0.78  second focus: battery + caption
  0.30  shell separates                  0.86  components return
  0.42  internals emerge                 0.95  reassembled, settle turn
                                         1.00  CTA handoff
```

Rules: beats are monotonic in `p`; first beat at 0 and last at 1; **something must visibly change within the first 0.05** (immediate feedback); captions attach to beats, and every caption's content also exists in the plain-DOM narrative (§10).

## 5. Rendering tiers and the never-flatten rule

**Tier A — real-time 3D (default).** GLB/glTF parts → Three.js or R3F; `p` drives transforms, materials, lights. Choose whenever a part hierarchy exists or can be modeled.
**Tier B — rendered frame sequence.** Blender/C4D render → WebP/AVIF frames → canvas scrub (the Apple AirPods technique). Choose for photoreal scenes too heavy for live rendering. Frames are still driven by the same beat map (`frame = round(p × (N−1))`); captions and landmarks stay real DOM.
**Tier C — video scrub.** `video.currentTime = p × duration`. Last resort only: seeking is imprecise and keyframe-dependent, reversal stutters, parts can't be addressed. Requires an all-keyframe (I-frame) encode.

**The asset rule: never flatten a usable multipart 3D product into video if the component hierarchy can be preserved.** A watch, phone, GPU, server, engine, drone, sneaker or robot with separable parts becomes an interactive scroll narrative (Tier A), not decorative footage. Downgrade tiers only for photorealism the GPU budget can't carry (→ B) or when the source simply isn't reconstructable (→ C).

## 6. GLB and part conventions

- **Hierarchy**: one root `product`; direct children are addressable parts named `part_<slug>` in disassembly order (`part_glass`, `part_screen`, `part_board`, `part_battery`, `part_shell_back`). Sub-assemblies nest one level max.
- **Pivots** sit at each part's *assembled* position; explosion is a translation from rest, so `explode = 0` is always exactly the assembled product.
- **Explosion vectors** live in a JSON sidecar (or glTF `extras`): `{ "part_glass": { "dir": [0,1,0], "dist": 1.2, "order": 1 } }` — per-part direction (unit), distance (in product-radius units), and stagger order. Configurable per component, ExplodeView-style.
- **Scale/units**: meters; product normalized so its bounding radius ≈ 1 — camera distances in recipes are multiples of it.
- **Compression**: Draco or Meshopt; textures KTX2 (fallback WebP) ≤ 2048px; PBR with one material per part so dim/highlight is a per-part `opacity`/`emissive` write, never a shared-material mutation.
- Author the black-background look in the scene (rim + key lights, dark env), not baked into textures, so packs can retint via `--ifx-grad-a/b` accent lights.

## 7. The scroll engine contract

`assets/scroll-scene.js` (`window.IFXScrollScene`) is dependency-free and renderer-agnostic — it computes progress and interpolated beat state; Three.js, canvas-sequence or video adapters consume it. GSAP ScrollTrigger can replace it 1:1 where already present (map `self.progress` to the same beat interpolation).

```js
const scene = IFXScrollScene.create({
  section: document.querySelector('#story'),   // tall pinned section
  beats: recipes['exploded-assembly'].beats,
  onUpdate(state, p, info) { /* write state.* into your renderer */ },
  onBeat(beat, dir) { /* captions, landmarks, aria-live */ },
});
```

Guarantees: passive listeners only (never preventDefault — no scroll hijacking); rAF-coalesced updates only while the section intersects; numeric fields eased between beats, discrete fields switched at beats; `prefers-reduced-motion` detected and (by default) progress quantized to beat states — stepped, still reversible; `destroy()` releases everything. Helpers: `lerp, remap, clamp, ease.*`.

## 8. UX contract (non-negotiable)

Field feedback on scroll-driven 3D sites is consistent: people abandon when scrolling feels dead and get disoriented when reversing misbehaves. Every scrollytelling scene therefore ships with:

1. **Immediate feedback** — visible change within the first 5% of the pin; never a long dead zone before the scene "starts".
2. **Reversible timeline** — scrolling up exactly rewinds; no one-way triggers, no re-fired entrance animations.
3. **Landmarks** — a progress rail with labeled beat dots that are real buttons (scroll-to on activation); current beat reflected in text.
4. **No scroll hijacking** — native scroll + `position: sticky`; wheel/touch are never captured or re-timed. (Smoothing via Lenis is acceptable; capturing is not.)
5. **Honest pin length** — 300–600vh desktop; more scroll than story is padding, less is whiplash.
6. **Reduced motion** — stepped beat states or a static poster + the full text narrative; parallax and particle drift removed.
7. **Mobile simplification** — pin ≤ 350vh, DPR ≤ 1.5, part count and lights reduced, captions become an inline stack; touch never fights vertical scroll.
8. **Escape hatch** — content after the pin is reachable by keyboard and a "skip story" link precedes the scene.

## 9. Performance budgets

Hero scene ≤ 150k triangles, ≤ 80 draw calls, textures ≤ 2048 KTX2/WebP, total 3D payload ≤ 6 MB (Tier B: frames ≤ 4 MB via AVIF/WebP ~85% quality, ≤ 160 frames, resolution-switched by viewport). Lazy-init on approach (IntersectionObserver, one viewport early); pause rendering when off-screen; cap `devicePixelRatio` at 2 (1.5 mobile); scene update ≤ 8 ms on a mid-tier phone. Preload strategy for Tier B: first + last frames immediately, the rest in idle time, decode ahead of the scrub direction.

## 10. Accessibility and honest duplication

The canvas is `aria-hidden`; the story exists in parallel as ordinary DOM: headings per act, the same captions and spec values in a plain section after the pin (the "spec sheet" duplicates every annotated number). Beat changes may announce politely (throttled) via a visually-hidden live region. Focus order ignores the scene entirely; the progress-rail buttons are the only interactive scene chrome. If WebGL is unavailable, render the poster + narrative — the page must still sell the product with zero JavaScript-driven motion.

Reference translation law applies here as everywhere: study the linked material for **beat timing, camera language, lighting-on-black, part choreography and annotation style** — never copy a specific product's model, footage, or composition.

# Component contracts

Use this contract before selecting or implementing any catalog element. The machine-readable catalog is `assets/component-contracts.json`, validated by `assets/component-contract.schema.json`; this document defines how to interpret and extend it.

## Contents

1. Contract fields
2. Selection rules
3. State contract
4. Composition rules
5. Extension procedure

## 1. Contract fields

Every catalog entry must define:

| Field | Requirement |
|---|---|
| `id` | Stable kebab-case identifier. |
| `family` | Navigation, input, data-display, visualization, feedback, overlay, content, action or shell; a catalog may additionally declare the surface-specific `mobile` or `extension` family. |
| `purpose` | User decision or task the element supports; never describe appearance alone. |
| `minimumSize` | Smallest useful width/height or touch target, with units and surface assumptions. |
| `requiredData` | Minimum fields, types, units, timestamps, provenance or state needed to render honestly. |
| `interactions` | Pointer, keyboard, touch and programmatic behavior, including disabled/busy behavior. |
| `accessibility` | Role/semantics, accessible name, focus rules, announcements and nonvisual equivalent. |
| `themeBehavior` | Semantic tokens, contrast-sensitive parts, forced-colors behavior and chart/color constraints. |
| `responsive` | Reflow, simplification, overflow and alternate presentation rules. |
| `states` | At least default, loading, empty, error and disabled when applicable; add stale/partial/permission states as needed. |
| `avoid` | Known misuse, deceptive treatment or condition that requires a different component. |

Treat minimum sizes as behavior thresholds, not fixed design dimensions. Content, zoom and platform text scaling can require more room.

When a multi-platform contract lists CSS px, iOS pt and Android dp together, select the unit for the current target rather than converting or averaging them. Surface-wide minimums still apply when they are stricter than an individual visual size.

## 2. Selection rules

1. Start from the user's question or task, then choose a component. Do not begin with a chart gallery.
2. Use the smallest component that preserves meaning and actionability.
3. Do not show precise values only through position, angle, area, color or animation.
4. Prefer a table for lookup and exact comparison; prefer a chart for pattern detection.
5. Pair compact visualization with value, unit, timeframe and change context.
6. Use one dominant metric per compact card. Secondary values must clarify, not compete.
7. Avoid nesting interactive controls inside another interactive control.
8. Do not compress an element below its minimum contract; switch to its responsive alternative.

## 3. State contract

For each selected component, explicitly map reachable states:

- **Loading:** preserve approximate final geometry and expose busy state without indefinite motion.
- **Empty:** explain why no data exists and offer the next useful action when one exists.
- **Error:** preserve context/input, explain impact and offer retry or recovery.
- **Stale:** show last-updated time and whether actions remain safe.
- **Partial:** distinguish missing series/fields from real zero values.
- **Permission:** state what access is needed, why and how to continue or decline.
- **Disabled:** keep the reason discoverable; do not rely on low opacity alone.
- **Success:** confirm the outcome without stealing focus or blocking continued work.

Live changes that materially affect a decision require an appropriate status announcement; high-frequency values should not flood assistive technology.

## 4. Composition rules

- Give the page one dominant decision area; supporting cards should form groups with shared alignment and rhythm.
- Align comparable numbers by baseline and use tabular numerals.
- Keep units, time windows and aggregation methods visible.
- Use consistent legends and series colors across a product.
- Do not repeat the same metric in multiple chart forms unless the second form answers a different question.
- Place controls near the content they affect and show filter scope.
- Preserve reading and focus order when visual order changes.
- Keep destructive and irreversible actions spatially and visually distinct.

## 5. Extension procedure

When adding a catalog element:

1. Define the user decision/task and identify why an existing element is insufficient.
2. Add a complete entry to the appropriate `component-contracts.json`.
3. Add benchmark coverage if the element introduces a new behavior family.
4. Add or extend validation for any deterministic safety rule.
5. Test light, dark, high-contrast, narrow, wide, zoomed, keyboard and reduced-motion behavior.

# Tool Routing — Capability-First Execution

Use this reference when a UI task depends on browser inspection, media creation, deployment, or an unfamiliar host. Choose tools by capability and contract rather than by product name.

## Contents

1. Capability inventory
2. Routing order
3. Media operations
4. Browser and visual validation
5. Deployment
6. Permission and failure handling

## 1. Capability inventory

At the start of the task, mark each capability as available, unavailable, or approval-gated:

| Capability | Typical use | Minimum safe contract |
|---|---|---|
| File read/search | inspect project and references | preserve unrelated user files |
| File edit/patch | implement UI | edit the smallest relevant scope |
| Shell/build | install, build, test, package | inspect commands and working directory first |
| Browser/preview | render and interact | do not submit or publish without request |
| Screenshot/image inspection | compare layout and references | verify the actual rendered artifact |
| Web research | current docs, standards, assets | prefer primary sources and honor licenses |
| Image retrieval | editorial or product imagery | keep source/usage rights clear |
| Image generation/editing | custom art, mockups, cutouts | ask before paid or bulk generation |
| Video/3D generation | hero loops or spatial assets | estimate cost and payload first |
| Deployment/hosting | publish a working build | require explicit user intent and verify rollback |

Do not infer a capability from a familiar product name. Inspect the tools the host actually exposes.

## 2. Routing order

Use this order:

1. Reuse repository-local assets, components, and scripts.
2. Use a host-native capability already available for the task.
3. Use an installed connector or MCP tool that matches the capability.
4. Use a local deterministic fallback.
5. Ask the user only when the missing capability blocks a material requirement.

Never fabricate a tool call, tool result, URL, screenshot, or successful deployment. If a preferred provider is unavailable, continue with the next valid route and disclose any material difference.

## 3. Media operations

Map the intent to the narrowest operation:

| Intent | Preferred operation | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| Understand an attachment | image/file inspection | ask the user to reattach if inaccessible |
| Find factual/reference imagery | licensed image search or web research | repository assets or procedural art |
| Create a new hero illustration | image generation | CSS/SVG/canvas composition |
| Modify an existing visual | image editing with the source attached | rebuild as code only if the user permits |
| Remove a background | background-removal/edit tool | CSS mask only for simple geometric subjects |
| Produce icons | code-native SVG when precision matters | generated raster only for illustrative icons |
| Produce a data diagram | HTML/SVG/chart library | never use generative imagery for exact data |

Before paid generation, bulk generation, video, or 3D, present the shot list and ask for approval unless the user's request already clearly authorizes it. Do not put provider credentials in generated client code.

## 4. Browser and visual validation

When a browser or preview is available:

1. start the project's documented development command;
2. wait for a healthy URL;
3. inspect console and network failures;
4. capture representative mobile and desktop views;
5. interact with navigation, forms, overlays, and primary flows;
6. compare against the brief and reference images;
7. iterate and repeat the affected checks.

When only screenshots are available, inspect them but do not claim interaction coverage. When no renderer is available, run build/static checks and state that visual QA remains unverified.

## 5. Deployment

Deploy only after an explicit request. Prefer:

1. the repository's existing deployment workflow;
2. an already-connected hosting provider selected by the user;
3. a reversible preview deployment;
4. documented manual steps when no deployment capability exists.

Before any production write, resolve the target project, branch, environment, and public URL. After deployment, read back the deployment state and open the URL when possible.

## 6. Permission and failure handling

- Treat payment, external writes, account changes, and publication as explicit boundaries.
- Preserve the host's sandbox and approval model; do not work around denied access.
- If a tool fails, inspect the error, retry only when safe and likely transient, then use a fallback.
- Do not replace a required capability with a lower-quality route when that would violate the user's acceptance criteria; stop and explain the blocker.
